title: ECMAScript Abstract Equality (==) Simulator
problemStatement: Implement `abstractEquals(x, y)` implementing the precise ECMAScript loose equality `==` rules without using the native `==` operator. Must handle null/undefined pairs, String/Number coercions, Boolean-to-number conversions, and Object-to-primitive conversions.
interviewTrap: When comparing a Boolean with anything else, the Boolean is coerced to a Number FIRST! So `[] == true` -> `[] == 1` -> `'' == 1` -> `0 === 1` -> `false`.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: The engine coerces primitives via internal algorithms. In loose equality (`==`), boolean values are first coerced to numbers, objects are coerced via `ToPrimitive(hint)`, and `null == undefined` is exclusively true.
stepByStepWalkthrough: 1. Initialize execution context and environment records for ECMA-262 7.2.14 Abstract Equality Comparison Algorithm.
2. Execute logic adhering to ECMAScript standard specification.
3. Verify invariant boundaries and edge conditions.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In JavaScript engines (e.g. V8), ECMA-262 7.2.14 Abstract Equality Comparison Algorithm is optimized via inline caches, heap contexts, and bytecode translation.
edgeCasesHandled: When comparing a Boolean with anything else, the Boolean is coerced to a Number FIRST! So `[] == true` -> `[] == 1` -> `'' == 1` -> `0 === 1` -> `false`.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Walk through the exact 12-step algorithm for Abstract Equality Comparison (==).
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: ECMA-262 §7.2.14 specifies: 1) Same type -> Strict Equality (===). 2) null == undefined -> true. 3) Number == String -> ToNumber(String). 4) Boolean == any -> ToNumber(Boolean) == any. 5) BigInt == String -> StringToBigInt. 6) Object == String/Number/BigInt -> ToPrimitive(Object) == primitive. 7) Any other combination -> false.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The definitive test of JavaScript specification mastery.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why does [] == ![] evaluate to true?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Step 1: `![]` evaluates unary NOT first; since arrays are truthy, `![]` becomes `false`. Expression is now `[] == false`. Step 2: Boolean on right triggers Rule 4: `ToNumber(false) === 0`. Expression is now `[] == 0`. Step 3: Object on left triggers Rule 6: `ToPrimitive([])` calls `[].toString()` which is `''`. Expression is now `'' == 0`. Step 4: String on left triggers Rule 3: `ToNumber('') === 0`. Expression is now `0 == 0`, which is `true`!
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The most famous JavaScript interview puzzle; testing whether candidate guesses or walks the formal spec.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why is === preferred in 100% of modern enterprise codebases?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: `===` (Strict Equality) performs NO coercion: if types differ, it immediately returns `false`. This eliminates the O(N) multi-step coercion cascades, improves JIT compiler inline caching, and prevents catastrophic bugs.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Ensures practical engineering judgment accompanies theoretical spec knowledge.

realWorldUseCases.description: Linters enforce strict equality across codebases to eliminate coercion vulnerabilities during code reviews.
The one accepted idiomatic exception in some codebases: `x == null` checks if `x` is either `null` OR `undefined` in a single check.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: if (val == null) return; // handles both null and undefined

howToExplain.opening: The Abstract Equality Comparison algorithm (==) performs recursive type conversions until types match, following strict priority rules defined in ECMA-262 §7.2.14.
keyPoints: Booleans are always coerced to numbers first (true -> 1, false -> 0).
Objects are coerced to primitives using ToPrimitive (valueOf then toString).
null and undefined equal each other and nothing else under ==.
Always use === to avoid the multi-step coercion pipeline and ensure type safety.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Understanding the exact steps of the equality algorithm turns apparent JavaScript quirks into predictable mechanical evaluations.
analogies: A multi-stage translation pipeline: English and French speakers translating through Latin until both speak the same dialect.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming [] == true evaluates to true because [] is truthy.
commonMistakes.why: In `[] == true`, `true` is coerced to `1`, and `[]` is coerced to `0`. `0 == 1` evaluates to `false`!
commonMistakes.correct: Remember that the == algorithm coerces booleans to numbers first, it does NOT evaluate truthiness.

followUpDeepDive.question: How does SameValueZero differ from Strict Equality (===)?
followUpDeepDive.answer: Strict equality (`===`) treats `NaN === NaN` as `false`, and `+0 === -0` as `true`. `SameValueZero` (used by `Map`, `Set`, and `Array.prototype.includes`) treats `NaN` as equal to `NaN`, allowing Maps to look up `NaN` keys accurately.
